info.bio: Grupo vocal femenino de la América de 1960, y el primero en tener un único número uno en el Billboard Hot 100. Los miembros del cuarteto fueron Shirley Owens, Doris Coley, Beverly Lee, y Addie" Micki "Harris. Formado en Nueva Jersey en 1958, inició una cadena de éxitos incluyendo "Baby it's you" , "Mama Said", "Foolish Little Girl", y el nº 1 en los Pop Hits "Will You Love Me Tomorrow"  y "Soldier Boy". Su "Sha La La" se convirtió en un éxito internacional versionándola el grupo británico Manfred Mann y dándoles un Top 5 hit en 1965.

scenes.name: Girl groups y Shangri-Las
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: Antes del beat, el estilo de los grupos femeninos dominó las listas americanas desde que las Shirelles llegaron al número 1 con «Will You Love Me Tomorrow» (1961): discos afilados, bailables y bien observados. «My Boyfriend’s Back» de las Angels y «You Don’t Own Me» de Lesley Gore eran declaraciones chocantes. Tras la invasión británica, los Shangri-Las de Red Bird lo prolongaron un par de años: chicas duras de Queens a las que George «Shadow» Morton dejaba ser ellas mismas en sinfonías de 45 rpm con gaviotas y motos, sobre romances condenados y tragedias familiares, «como la chica corriente». Su último single en Red Bird, «Past, Present and Future» (mayo de 1966), sobre la «Sonata Claro de luna», es un examen desolado de un desastre amoroso.

scenes.name: Antes del diluvio
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: La «edad oscura» del rock'n'roll: los rebeldes son sustituidos por ídolos adolescentes educados y el Brill Building devuelve el poder a los compositores profesionales. Pero en esos años se incuban la revolución futura: la guitarra fuzz de Link Wray, los bailes de moda (el twist), el rock instrumental de guitarras (Duane Eddy, Ventures, Shadows), el calipso y el primer ska, el doo-wop más inventivo (Coasters, Drifters, Five Royales), el nacimiento del soul (Sam Cooke, Ray Charles, Motown, Stax), el estudio como instrumento de Joe Meek y el surf de los Beach Boys y del «muro de sonido» de Phil Spector.

podcast.title: Decca Records Contract and Drop
podcast.body: After "I Met Him On A Sunday" found minor local success, Decca Records bought The Shirelles' contract from Florence Greenberg. Although the song reached number 50 on the charts, their subsequent two singles for Decca were unsuccessful, leading the label to drop them. "They managed to get it to number 50 on the chart but the two singles they recorded for Deca after that didn't have any success and the label dropped them."

podcast.title: Discovery by Mary Jane Greenberg
podcast.body: After performing "I Met Him On A Sunday" at their school talent contest, they impressed Mary Jane Greenberg, a fellow student. Mary Jane insisted that the girls meet her mother, Florence Greenberg, who would later become their manager and record label owner, despite the girls' attempts to avoid her initially. "In particular one of the girls there, Mary Jane Greenberg, insisted that the girls come and meet her mother, Florence."

podcast.title: Formation and Original Name - The Parakeets
podcast.body: Shirley Owens, Doris Coley, Addie Harris, and Beverly Lee met at school in Pasey, New Jersey, about 16 miles from New York, and formed a group called The Parakeets. This name, Spanish for "little birds," was in line with the trend of early do-wop groups often being named after birds. "Shirley Owens, Doris Coley, Adi Harris and Beverly Lee met at school and formed a group called the Parqueos which is apparently Spanish for little birds."

podcast.title: Influence of Luther Dixon
podcast.body: After Florence Greenberg started Scepter Records and re-signed The Shirelles, the label's A&R director Wally Roker introduced her to Luther Dixon. Dixon's involvement as a staff writer and producer, and his eventual relationship with Greenberg, dramatically changed the group's fortunes, leading to their biggest hits, including their first Top 40 and number one singles. "but then a change in SEPTRA's staffing changed everything not just for the Chirrells but for the world of music."

"R&B girl groups. Like the Sherels."

podcast.title: Maternity Leave and Replacement Singers
podcast.body: As the group members started families, one or another member often had to be replaced for road shows while on maternity leave. During these times, session singer Dionne Warwick, who Burt Bacharach was producing for Scepter, filled in for them. "It didn't help that the girls were starting families, and at various times, one or other member had to be replaced on the road while they were on maternity leave."

podcast.title: Pioneering Girl Group Influence
podcast.body: The Shirelles were historically mistreated by their record company and largely ignored by rock historians due to their success falling within the 1958-1964 period, which is often dismissed as uninteresting. However, their success was pivotal, setting the template for the booming girl group phenomenon of the 1960s and profoundly influencing groups like The Supremes, The Marvelettes, The Crystals, and The Ronettes. "They made some of the most important records of the sixties, and it was their success that led to the great booming girl groups of the next few years."

podcast.title: Post-Scepter Career and Multiple Lineups
podcast.body: Despite the legal troubles that effectively ended their hit-making career, The Shirelles continued to perform in various lineups, with members coming and going, until the early 1980s. At that point, the original members went their separate ways, but each started their own version of The Shirelles. "They remained together in one line up of another, with members coming in and going, until the early eighties, when they all went their separate ways, though they all started their own line-ups of Chirrells."

podcast.title: Reluctance to Professional Singing
podcast.body: The group that became the most successful early girl group never wanted to be professional singers and had to be coerced at every stage. Their first public performance was a punishment for singing in gym class instead of paying attention, leading their teacher to make them perform in a school talent contest. "Oddly the group that became the most successful of the early girl groups and the one that more than any other set the template for all those that would follow never wanted to become professional singers and almost had to be forced against their will at every stage."

podcast.title: Renaming to The Shirelles
podcast.body: After signing with Florence Greenberg's TRA Records, The Parakeets were renamed The Shirelles. The new name was derived from Shirley Owens, the lead singer, with an "-elles" ending to evoke other popular groups like The Chantels. "The Perqueos were also renamed to the Chirrells after Shirley Owens but with the Al ending to be reminiscent of the Shang Tells and that was the name that would be known back from that point on."

podcast.title: Rights to the Name
podcast.body: Today, Shirley Owens performs under her married name, Shirley Alston Reeves, with her group "Shirley Alston Reeves and her Shirelles." Beverly Lee, another original member, owns the rights to perform as "The Shirelles" with no modifiers. "These days, Shirley Toys under her married name, as Shirley Alston Reeves and her Chirrells, while Beverly Lee owns the rights to Toys the Chirrells with no modifiers."

podcast.title: Royalty Dispute and Lawsuits
podcast.body: The Shirelles discovered that Florence Greenberg had lied to them about their royalties. They had been told their earnings were being placed into a trust for them until they turned twenty-one, but no such trust existed, and Greenberg had been keeping their money. This led them to file lawsuits against Scepter Records, but remaining signed to the label, they were unable to record for anyone else, which effectively destroyed their career. "They've been told that their royalties were being put into a trust for them for when they turned twenty-one, but they discovered that no such trust existed, and Greenberg had just been keeping their money."
